articles.body:
Jordan’s prime minister represents king at funeral for eight of the church attack victims as hunt for gunmen continues.

Thousands of mourners have gathered for the funerals of eight of the victims of a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan, with Prime Minister Jafar Hassan also in attendance.

The burials on Sunday were beside St George’s Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud, southwest of the capital, Amman, two days after attackers opened fire during another funeral there.

Recommended Stories

list of 2 items

- list 1 of 2Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?

- list 2 of 2Jordan’s King Abdullah orders firm response after deadly church attack

Nine people were killed and dozens wounded in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority, prompting three days of national mourning.

The ninth victim, Mohammed al-Qasous, is due to be buried on Monday, his family told the AFP news agency.

Coffins wrapped in Jordanian flags were carried through crowds gathered around the church in Karak province, as priests led prayers and security personnel stood guard.

Prime Minister Hassan attended the service alongside government ministers and senior military and civilian officials, according to Jordan’s state news agency, Petra.

Thousands of citizens also participated in the funeral procession, Petra said.

Among those caught in Friday’s shooting was Sahar al-Halsa, who told the Reuters news agency from her nearby home that she sheltered behind a pillar as gunfire erupted and people screamed.

When she rushed outside, she found her cousin Assem lying wounded.

“Assem, Assem, my darling, answer me,” she recalled calling to him. He briefly opened his eyes before dying, she said.

Father Yohanna Hamati told AFP that about 170 to 200 people were at the church for Friday’s funeral when firing began outside.

The mourners initially struggled to understand what was happening, he said, before people began rushing into the church to escape.

By Saturday, bullet holes remained in the walls and wooden pews, and windows had been shattered.

Church workers were cleaning away blood as villagers prepared to bury the dead. Jordanian authorities have described the attack as “extremist terrorism”.

King Abdullah, who visited some of the wounded in hospital on Friday, has promised a forceful response and the assailants are still being sought.

Officials say they have not established whether the attackers were connected to an armed group and no organisation has claimed responsibility.

The violence has also drawn expressions of solidarity across religious lines. Christians account for about 3 percent of Jordan’s largely Muslim population and AFP reported that Muslims were among those wounded.

Young volunteers visited a hospital in Karak with flowers and a message reading, “Our loss is one”.

The mourning reached Washington, DC, on Sunday, where members of the Jordanian community lit candles outside their country’s embassy.

Jordan’s ambassador to the US, Dina Kawar, told those gathered that efforts to stir religious division were “bound to fail”. Back in Hamoud, Father Hamati appealed for unity, stressing that Muslims had also suffered in the attack.

“We make no distinction between Muslim and Christian,” he told AFP.

articles.title: How is the US-Israeli war on Iran causing havoc in Europe?
articles.summary: Rising energy costs and protests are sharpening European opposition to renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
articles.preview: Rising energy costs and protests are sharpening European opposition to renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran. Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe. Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.
articles.body:
Rising energy costs and protests are sharpening European opposition to renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

Several Western European nations have expressed their opposition to the potential resumption of the Iran war, as spiralling global oil prices have worsened the cost of living crisis across Europe.

Countries such as Germany and the UK, among other major powers, which initially remained silent on the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran, have aired their views, calling for diplomacy to end the war which has disrupted global oil supplies.

Continued disruption to energy supplies is pushing up household costs as winter in Europe approaches, adding fuel to protests over living standards that have engulfed European capitals in recent weeks.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Sunday drew attention to what he described as a shift in Germany’s position on attacks against Iran.

In a post on X, Baghaei recalled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s remarks during Israel’s June 2025 military campaign: “This is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”

He contrasted those words with German officials’ recent warnings against renewed attacks and calls to prevent further escalation, before citing Friedrich Schiller’s The Maid of Orleans, quoting a passage that portrays reason being helplessly dragged towards an abyss by the forces of madness.

Experts say Baghaei’s remarks reflect a broader shift across Europe, where leaders are increasingly questioning their support for the US-Israeli war on Iran.

With Washington reportedly preparing options for renewed attacks, what would further escalation mean for Europe and could the war further strain already frayed relations with the United States?

Here is what we know.

How has Europe’s position changed?

When the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28 , the leaders of Britain, France and Germany issued a joint statement condemning Iran’s retaliatory strikes on countries across the region. “We condemn Iranian attacks on countries in the region in the strongest terms,” British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, French President Emmanuel Macron and Merz said.

Their statement did not condemn the opening US-Israeli attacks. However, it called for negotiations to follow. Nearly eight months into the war, European governments are now explicitly warning against another military campaign.

On Friday, the foreign ministers of Britain, France, Germany and Italy met their counterparts from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in Istanbul to discuss the conflict and the Strait of Hormuz. Further escalation between Iran and the US “would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

“And so the first thing this group of eight countries … will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region,” he added.

The warnings against new attacks do not necessarily mean European governments have abandoned their positions on Iran’s nuclear programme or regional activities, but they do show a change of position and have revealed that European governments are not united in their approach to the Iran war.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has consistently opposed the US-Israeli campaign. At this month’s European summit, he again described the war as “illegal, unjust and unjustified”, linking it to Europe’s mounting economic costs.

Western countries have opposed Iran’s nuclear programme, which Tehran says is for civilian purposes only. European countries were part of the landmark 2015 nuclear deal with Iran that limited Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. But during his first term in 2018, United States President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal. Both the US and Israel invoked Iran’s nuclear programme to launch their attack in February.

Have European bases been used?

Europe’s divisions have been particularly visible over access to military bases and airspace. “We did not participate in these strikes, but are in close contact with our international partners, including the United States, Israel and partners in the region,” said the February 28 statement from Britain, France and Germany.

But non-participation in the opening attacks did not mean European countries would uniformly refuse support for subsequent operations. Germany said early in the war that it would not restrict US use of its bases, including Ramstein, a major American military hub.

Britain initially withheld permission for the opening attacks. However, it authorised US use of British bases for what London described as specific, limited defensive strikes against Iranian facilities involved in attacks on regional allies. Then, after initial reluctance, Britain expanded that permission to include operations against missile sites and capabilities being used to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

France allowed US support aircraft at Istres, while saying they would support the defence of regional partners rather than participate in attacks on Iran. It later blocked a weapons flight to Israel connected to the campaign. Spain went further. After refusing permission for attacks from the jointly operated Rota and Moron bases, Madrid closed its airspace to US aircraft involved in the war.

Those were different restrictions with different purposes, rather than a single European refusal to cooperate, but they provoked Trump. Calling Spain “terrible”, he threatened to cut off trade and said Washington wanted “nothing to do with Spain”.

The dispute has therefore exposed a widening argument over whether alliance commitments require European governments to facilitate a war they did not choose.

Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera: “As to whether the war might push European leaders to openly challenge Trump, and limit support, it is certainly possible. What was initially a diplomatic disagreement is turning into something that has much more direct … and we could see increased resistance to any support from European countries.”

High prices and protest

After Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said there was “renewed hope for the people of Iran”. She also warned then that instability could push the region into a spiral of violence. But by October 16, the costs to Europe had become central to her message. “Households and industry are paying the price for a war far beyond our borders,” she said after an EU summit.

According to von der Leyen, Europe’s bill for imported fossil fuels had increased by 106 billion euros, while gas prices had risen about 140 percent since late February and diesel prices had doubled.

Disruption to Gulf supplies and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have also caused energy prices to spike. Brent crude settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, before the war began. It reached $126.41 at the end of April and remains well above $100 a barrel, with no sign of falling any time soon.

“For Europe, there is the economic interest as well, knowing it would further take a toll on energy markets, pushing up prices at a time when European countries are going into winter and the pushback to that,” Julie Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera.

Hilborne added that “there is an impact as well on food and fertiliser … The Persian Gulf is a hub for nitrogen-based fertilisers and disruptions have sent prices of urea up by something like 70 percent. Also, supply chains are feeling the impact as well, as shipping companies are facing large increases in their insurance premiums and/or need to reroute to longer journeys”.

“I would say that the Iranian war has had a direct, measurable and quite a rapid impact on European prices,” he added.

The search for relief from the energy crisis has created further friction, with Washington pressing European governments to release emergency diesel stocks, while Trump eased restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to lower prices. That move provoked criticism from Ukraine and its supporters, who warned that renewed energy revenues would strengthen Moscow’s war effort.

But some of the sharpest political consequences are unfolding closer to home. Protests over living costs, housing, wages and public services have been seen across France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Albania. Their causes vary, and they do not constitute a single coordinated movement, but experts say the cost of living crisis, compounded by price rises caused by the Iran war, is a common thread that unites the protesters across the continent.

Donatella della Porta, a sociologist and political scientist, told Al Jazeera that opposition to war was central to recent protests by young people across Europe, alongside anger over military spending at the expense of welfare.

She pointed to opposition to military recruitment in schools, weapons-related university research and the use of ports to transport arms, linking those concerns to wider fears about the future.

“Especially the young protesters are afraid that their future will be stolen not only by global warming but also by wars in which they will be sent to die on the battlefield,” she said.

“Young people also connect wars with genocide, having often been socialised into politics during the large protests against the Israeli genocide of the Palestinians.”

articles.body:
Due funzionari iraniani, uno dei quali membro dei Pasdaran, hanno detto al New York Times che l'ampliamento degli obiettivi di Teheran in caso di attacco include anche diplomatici e personale Usa. I funzionari, che hanno chiesto di rimanere anonimi, hanno confermato le notizie del Dipartimento di Stato relative al complotto iraniano volto a colpire cittadini americani.

I responsabili hanno difeso il piano: Israele e gli Stati Uniti "hanno ucciso decine di funzionari iraniani e alcuni loro familiari". A loro avviso, gli attacchi contro gli americani sono "leciti". Non è chiaro, tuttavia, se dispongano dei mezzi necessari per farlo.

Intanto da Teheran arriva un altro avvertimento: "Nulla tornerà allo stato in cui si trovava prima delle due recenti guerre, in particolare per quanto riguarda lo Stretto di Hormuz", afferma il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi, aggiungendo che "la guerra in corso ha cambiato tutto. Le rotte attraverso lo Stretto di Hormuz non saranno più quelle di un tempo".

Araghchi ha inoltre affermato che l'Iran ha sottolineato agli intermediari che la guerra deve cessare su tutti i fronti della regione, "altrimenti la pace rimarrà irraggiungibile".

Intanto Teheran ha attaccato con droni alcune postazioni curde anti-iraniane a Erbil, nel nord Iraq. Lo riferisce Fars. In precedenza erano state prese di mira basi del gruppo Komala nella regione del Balisan

articles.summary: A breve in Israele e negli Stati Uniti gli elettori decideranno il futuro politico di due uomini che ricoprono un ruolo cruciale nelle crisi del momento, Benjamin Netanyahu e Donald Trump
articles.preview: Due elezioni imminenti, che si svolgeranno a pochi giorni di distanza, rischiano di avere un peso considerevole sul clima internazionale. articles.body:
Due elezioni imminenti, che si svolgeranno a pochi giorni di distanza, rischiano di avere un peso considerevole sul clima internazionale. In Israele si voterà il 27 ottobre, mentre negli Stati Uniti i seggi apriranno il 3 novembre. In entrambi i paesi gli elettori decideranno il futuro politico di due uomini che ricoprono un ruolo cruciale nelle crisi del momento, Benjamin Netanyahu e Donald Trump.

Netanyahu si gioca la guida del governo in una votazione che per l’ennesima volta si è trasformata in un referendum sulla sua persona. Ma c’è una differenza rispetto al passato: quelle di martedì prossimo saranno le prime elezioni politiche dopo l’attacco di Hamas del 7 ottobre 2023. In Israele una parte del dibattito è incentrata sulla possibilità che Netanyahu sapesse in anticipo dell’attacco di Hamas e sul fallimento della sicurezza in quella giornata traumatica. La questione palestinese, invece, è sostanzialmente assente dai dibattiti, nonostante i settantamila morti di Gaza e le violenze incessanti dei coloni in Cisgiordania.

Il nome di Donald Trump non sarà presente sulle schede delle elezioni di metà mandato, ma il risultato del voto sarà comunque un giudizio sui due anni trascorsi alla Casa Bianca. Per i repubblicani è un passaggio che si annuncia molto difficile, al punto che l’unica incognita riguarda la portata della vittoria democratica e il modo in cui Trump gestirà la sconfitta (ammesso che sia capace di farlo) nella seconda parte del suo mandato.

I due voti sono segnati dalle guerre. Per Trump quella più importante è chiaramente la guerra in Iran, in cui si ritrova impantanato con le conseguenze che conosciamo per il prezzo dell’energia. L’aumento del costo della vita è il tema principale per gli elettori statunitensi, malgrado tutti gli sforzi del presidente per distogliere l’attenzione e dare l’impressione di lavorare per risolvere il problema.

In tutto questo, il riavvicinamento di Trump a Putin è passato dalla cancellazione di alcune sanzioni alla Russia e da un nuovo tentativo di costringere l’Ucraina a capitolare. Il 21 ottobre l’inviato statunitense Steve Witkoff ha addirittura dichiarato che Vladimir Putin è un “umanista”, una parola oscena in un momento in cui i missili cadono sui civili di Kiev.

Se per Trump le guerre rappresentano un tormento, per Netanyahu sono linfa vitale, tanto che il primo ministro sembra convinto di aver bisogno di scatenarne un’altra. Dopo aver provato invano all’inizio di ottobre a riprendere i bombardamenti contro l’Iran (fermato all’ultimo momento da Washington), il 21 ottobre Netanyahu ha riesumato i toni allarmisti per accusare Teheran di aver rilanciato il suo programma nucleare, minacciando di distruggerlo. Il primo ministro israeliano è fortemente tentato dall’idea di bombardare l’Iran a pochi giorni dal voto.

Affinché il clima cambi in modo significativo bisognerebbe che la coalizione di estrema destra guidata da Netanyahu perdesse le elezioni e che negli Stati Uniti i repubblicani perdessero entrambe le camere del congresso. In uno scenario di questo tipo un cambio di governo in Israele non garantirebbe affatto un approccio diverso ai vari fronti aperti nella regione, ma quanto meno creerebbe possibilità che oggi sono impensabili in un contesto di ossessione per la sicurezza.

Detto questo, è a Washington che bisognerà osservare attentamente le conseguenze del voto. Se Trump perderà il congresso (sempre che accetti il verdetto delle urne), dovrà fare i conti con un reale contrappeso al suo potere, oltre a incontrare una maggiore resistenza all’interno del Partito repubblicano. In questo senso vale la pena notare che il suo riavvicinamento a Putin è piuttosto malvisto.

In un editoriale pubblicato il 22 ottobre, il Wall Street Journal, di solito tutt’altro che ostile ai repubblicani, ha sottolineato che tra due settimane Trump potrebbe diventare una lame duck, un’anatra zoppa, ovvero un presidente con poteri dimezzati. Forse questa è l’unica buona notizia del momento.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it

articles.title: L’estrema destra sta capitalizzando sui disordini in Francia e Italia
articles.summary: Online le narrazioni xenofobe di “guerra etnica” o “assalto all’Occidente” sono sempre più sdoganate
articles.preview: Il 19 ottobre 2026 il noto streamer statunitense e commentatore politico Zack Hoyt (conosciuto con il nome di “Asmongold”), 3,5 milioni di follower su Twitch, ha fatto una diretta in cui reagisce e commenta mentre guarda alcuni filmati dei disordini avvenuti tra il 17 e il 18 ottobre in varie città italiane nel corso delle manifestazioni contro il carovita. Pubblicato poi su YouTube col titolo “What the f**k is happening in Italy??” (“Che ca**o sta succedendo in Italia??”), il video ha già totalizzato quasi 1,7 milioni di visualizzazioni.
articles.body:
Il 19 ottobre 2026 il noto streamer statunitense e commentatore politico Zack Hoyt (conosciuto con il nome di “Asmongold”), 3,5 milioni di follower su Twitch, ha fatto una diretta in cui reagisce e commenta mentre guarda alcuni filmati dei disordini avvenuti tra il 17 e il 18 ottobre in varie città italiane nel corso delle manifestazioni contro il carovita. Pubblicato poi su YouTube col titolo “What the f**k is happening in Italy??” (“Che ca**o sta succedendo in Italia??”), il video ha già totalizzato quasi 1,7 milioni di visualizzazioni. Affermatosi inizialmente come streamer del videogioco World of Warcraft, col tempo Hoyt ha attirato un pubblico molto vasto che lo segue per ascoltare le sue opinioni, orientate verso l’estrema destra.

Per mezz’ora Hoyt mostra video di saccheggi e vandalismi di ogni genere, e risponde ai messaggi che arrivano in diretta. Secondo Hoyt l’Italia si troverebbe in una situazione apocalittica, sull’orlo di una guerra civile portata avanti da un corpo estraneo alla società italiana, impegnato a distruggerne lo stile di vita. Quando qualche follower accenna alla precarietà generazionale e alle disparità di classe, una delle chiavi di lettura con cui analisti ed economisti stanno provando a spiegare dati alla mano le ragioni di tanta rabbia, Hoyt è categorico: «non ci dovrebbe essere disparità di classe, perché queste persone non dovrebbero nemmeno stare a casa nostra». La soluzione? Hoyt invoca contro i partecipanti ai disordini un approccio simile a quello duro e autoritario con cui il presidente del Salvador Nayib Bukele, popolarissimo negli ambienti della destra internazionale, ha combattuto le gang criminali del suo Paese – un approccio suggerito da Bukele stesso.

Il video di Hoyt rappresenta perfettamente il modo con cui l’estrema destra internazionale sta provando a raccontare i riots avvenuti in varie città italiane e francesi il 17 e il 18 ottobre: una crisi esistenziale dell’Occidente, la prova che il multiculturalismo ha fallito e la necessità di salvare le nostre società dai cittadini con background migratorio o di seconda generazione, eventualmente «remigrandoli tutti». Tuttavia, Hoyt non sembra costruire questa narrazione da solo. Durante la diretta, mentre lo streamer passa da un video all’altro, si intravede una lista dei link che sta seguendo, che è uno spaccato dei canali che in questi giorni hanno contribuito di più a diffondere una narrazione etno-nazionalista, scatenare panico e diffondere odio.

La rete di account di estrema destra

Da quando l’allora Twitter è stato acquistato, nel 2022, da Elon Musk, oltre al cambio del nome in X, la piattaforma social ha ridotto drasticamente la moderazione dei contenuti e si è trasformata in megafono dell’estrema destra. Non è un caso che tutti i link nella lista rimandano a X. Compare l’aggregatore di notizie polacco xenofobo e ultraconservatore Visegrad24, noto per diffondere disinformazione su svariati temi, un cui post sull’incendio del Municipio di Limoges è stato ripreso anche dal vice-presidente statunitense JD Vance; un video con più di 14 milioni di visualizzazioni di un account di propaganda MAGA e anti-immigrazione secondo cui un cittadino italiano, esasperato dalla situazione, ha affrontato da solo i saccheggiatori – in realtà analizzando il video Facta ha identificato l’uomo in un carabiniere in borghese.

Nella dieta mediatica di Hoyt spiccano anche due account italiani: uno è @FantomasRitorna, un profilo italiano di estrema destra attivo da diversi anni, che nonostante un seguito tutto sommato marginale, ha postato in questi giorni video dei saccheggi che hanno raccolto singolarmente più di sette milioni di visualizzazioni. L’altro è Radio Genoa, un account italiano in lingua inglese che in questi anni si è affermato a livello internazionale come uno dei più noti divulgatori di messaggi d’odio, razzismo, islamofobia e disinformazione a tema immigrazione. Con i disordini in Francia e in Italia, Radio Genoa sta avendo un ruolo importante nell’amplificare questa visione apocalittica. Solo per fare alcuni esempi, nei tweet che accompagnano i video degli ultimi giorni Radio Genoa scrive che “l’Europa è nel caos totale”, “questa Francia non ha futuro” e “Milano è perduta”.

Radio Genoa ha anche spinto e diffuso l’idea che dietro gli scontri ci sia una matrice religiosa: in un video che ha quasi cinque milioni di visualizzazioni su X, si vede un oggetto in fiamme in una strada antistante il Duomo di Milano, con la chiesa sullo sfondo distante centinaia di metri. Ma il commento è il seguente: «L’Italia come la Francia. Davanti al Duomo di Milano. Un simbolo della cristianità sotto assedio  Questa è una guerra alla nostra storia, alla nostra cultura, alle nostre tradizioni e alla nostra identità». In un altro post scrive che i cristiani sono sotto attacco ovunque, per poi aggiungere: «Questi criminali – nordafricani – hanno preso di mira il duomo di Milano. Il video lo mostra chiaramente». In realtà il video mostra un ragazzo che passa in una via laterale del Duomo di Milano mentre spruzza in aria il contenuto di un estintore.

Radio Genoa non è nuova a diffondere contenuti falsi, decontestualizzati o fuorvianti, ma la frequenza con cui l’ha fatto in questi giorni è notevole: oltre ai video già citati, in cui il Duomo sarebbe stato assediato da manifestanti islamisti, l’account ha diffuso molto altro materiale teso a seminare panico nell’opinione pubblica. Un video del 18 ottobre creato con l’intelligenza artificiale mostra la mostra la Torre Eiffel in fiamme, con il testo: «Parigi, molto, molto presto».

Su chi gestisce Radio Genoa fino a qualche anno fa non si sapeva molto, anche se un’indagine di Facta del 2023 aveva permesso di aggiungere qualche dettaglio importante. Nel 2024 anche il programma televisivo di giornalismo investigativo olandese Pointer si era messo sulle sue tracce, attirato dal fatto che il politico di estrema destra Geert Wilders condividesse frequentemente i contenuti dell’account. L’inchiesta aveva ricondotto il profilo su X a una persona, originaria della Liguria, chiamata Antonio Mastantuono. Lo stesso Mastantuono è successivamente venuto allo scoperto nel 2024, rivelando di essere oggetto di un’indagine da parte della magistratura italiana per incitamento all’odio, ottenendo per questo la solidarietà del senatore della Lega Claudio Borghi.

Da allora l’account è cresciuto, e la sua influenza come canale di propaganda anti-immigrazione è diventata evidente. Qualche giorno fa l’account X di Radio Genoa ha annunciato di aver raddoppiato con un nuovo sito. Allo stesso tempo, ha chiarito che «in segno di rispetto per @ElonMusk, che ci ha restituito la libertà di parola, @RadioGenoa non aprirà mai profili su Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube o Telegram.  Finché Elon proteggerà la libertà di parola, resteremo al 100% su X. La lealtà conta».

Intanto sui social continua a rimbalzare questa realtà parallela: stando a un video su X da 1,8 milioni di visualizzazioni postato da un account sudamericano di destra la città di Bologna «è stata completamente devastata». Altri account, condividendo le stesse immagini, hanno rincarato dicendo che «Bologna ha vissuto una delle peggiori notti della sua vita», o è «diventata una zona di guerra». In realtà a Bologna gli scontri con la polizia sono avvenuti quasi esclusivamente nell’area circostante la stazione ferroviaria.

La strumentalizzazione delle proteste francesi

In Francia, dove da tempo attivisti e politici di estrema destra sono riusciti a trovare spazio all’interno dei media mainstream, i movimenti estremisti stanno sfruttando l’occasione per spostare ancora di più il confine del dicibile, e raccontare ciò che è successo nei giorni passati come una guerra etnica. Il caso più evidente è quello della giovane attivista di estrema destra Thaïs d’Escufon, i cui video stanno circolando molto online, al punto che il senatore repubblicao Ted Cruz ne ha condiviso uno con i suoi sette milioni di follower. «L’unica soluzione pacifica è rimandarli nei loro Paesi d’origine che amano così tanto. Non possiamo coesistere. Saremo noi, o loro», ha detto l’attivista. D’Escufon è stata la portavoce del gruppo suprematista Génération identitaire dal 2018 fino al suo scioglimento da parte del governo francese nel 2021. Génération identitaire aveva ricevuto in passato delle donazioni anche da Brenton Tarrant, il terrorista responsabile dell’attentato nella Moschea di Christchurch in Nuova Zelanda, costato la vita a 51 persone. Eppure un profilo come il suo, che chiede apertamente l’uccisione dei manifestanti, sta scalando la piramide mediatica e trovando casse di risonanza sempre più vaste.

In questi giorni le proteste sono state sfruttate anche a fini politici attraverso un ampio ricorso all’intelligenza artificiale, usata per creare contenuti di disinformazione di grande impatto. Il caso più noto è la falsa foto di due ottantenni derubati dai manifestanti, resa virale da un profilo su X che in passato aveva già diffuso disinformazione contro attivisti per la Palestina e il partito di estrema sinistra La France Insoumise.

Il presidente francese Emmanuel Macron intanto ha condannato la strumentalizzazione della situazione francese, affermando che «alcuni leader, «nel pieno delle campagne elettorali, sia qui nella regione sia dall’altra parte dell’Atlantico  stanno usando il nostro Paese per le loro campagne politiche». Macron ha anche denunciato la circolazione di immagini generate dall’intelligenza artificiale «che raffigurano scene che in realtà non sono mai accadute in Francia. C’è stato chi ha sostenuto che fossimo stati invasi da orde di migranti e islamisti, cosa assolutamente falsa». In molti hanno subito pensato alle parole del presidente statunitense Donald Trump, che qualche giorno prima aveva commentato che «se l’Europa non chiude i suoi confini e non ne espelle i criminali, come le persone che stanno protestando, l’Europa è finita».

Tuttavia, prese di posizione analoghe sono arrivate sui social anche dal premier polacco Donald Tusk e il primo ministro ungherese Péter Magyar: commentando le immagini provenienti da Parigi, entrambi hanno parlato della necessità di confini sicuri e della difesa dell’Europa dall’immigrazione illegale. È la prova che la narrazione identitaria e xenofoba sulle proteste è ormai riuscita a far breccia anche tra i leader conservatori meno radicali.

articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
articles.preview: Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.
articles.body:
Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching.

Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

OpenAI has taken several stumbles

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “super app.” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

Apple’s Siri AI

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs. This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Microsoft’s Recall

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22.

Humane AI Pin

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

Rabbit R1

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down.

Character.ai

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

articles.body:
On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies, as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials.

Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.

Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.

The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.

The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
articles.summary: A new study found Grok's AI overwhelmingly recommends Republican candidates while OpenAI's GPT favors Democrats, with the two AI models disagreeing in more than 90% of nearly 500 election races.
articles.preview: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.
articles.body:
Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.

Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew, and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral.

The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.

There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.

“ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.”

SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment.

Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions.

“It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics.

“If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said.

Previous research has raised similar concerns.

The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing.

The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.

Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%.

GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.)

The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.

ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.

The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote.

Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72.

“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.

One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.

Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat.

When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.”

The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine.

Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections.

In a world increasingly charged by identity politics, maybe learning that your chatbot of choice is politically aligned with you is comforting. But for those who still want the opportunity to review each candidate’s stance and make their own choices, here are some resources:

- Vote.gov

- League of Women Voters’ vote411.org

- Ballotpedia

- VoteSmart

- FEC.gov and OpenSecrets

- State and county election offices

- Candidates’ websites and local news

articles.body:
It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook.

Not that I believe for a second that Apple will actually make a 2-in-1 convertible.

Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.

The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse.

The Yoga 9n’s included stylus works for note-taking and drawing on its excellent OLED display, but you can also use it on the haptic trackpad for a Wacom-like experience, without blocking the screen with your hand. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient

I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Lenovo’s stylus relies on USB-C charging, which is fine, but not as convenient as always having it charged and ready to go while attached to your laptop.

I don’t expect Apple to make a standard convertible laptop after all this time. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky.

My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. The HomeView’s lack of apps is perplexing. The iPhone Duo is a little messy. Current MacBooks are so great, it’s easy to forget the butterfly keyboard fiasco wasn’t all that long ago. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
articles.summary: OpenAI will cut frontier models off from the internet weeks after one of its engineers said that solution wouldn't work.
articles.preview: On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access. The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet.
articles.body:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.

The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”

“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”

The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”

Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

articles.title: Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
articles.summary: Bangladesh expected to surpass India's per capita GDP this year, but that's not the complete economic picture.
articles.preview: Bangladesh is expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but the complete economic picture is a mix of success stories and new challenges. Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to be higher than that of Asia’s third largest economy, India, this year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). GDP is a measure of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. India’s GDP is nearly eight times larger than Bangladesh’s.
articles.body:
Bangladesh is expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but the complete economic picture is a mix of success stories and new challenges.

Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to be higher than that of Asia’s third largest economy, India, this year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

GDP is a measure of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. India’s GDP is nearly eight times larger than Bangladesh’s. But its neighbour’s per capita GDP, which is GDP divided by the total population, is expected to surpass that of India, the world’s most populous nation.

The projected 2026 per capita GDP of Bangladesh, home to about 175 million people, is $2,886, compared with $2,749 in India as Dhaka emerges as one of South Asia’s notable economic success stories over the past two decades. Bangladesh’s economy is currently larger than that of Pakistan, from which Dhaka seceded in 1971.

Experts link the rise to the country’s $38bn garment industry, remittances and growing participation of women in the workforce.

But high inflation and slowing growth are now putting that progress under pressure. Meanwhile, the Indian economy is expected to grow by 7 percent this year, compared with 3.6 percent in Bangladesh.

So how should one read these numbers, and what do they really mean for millions of people living in these countries?

What’s in the IMF report?

The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook report underscores differences in how the Indian and Bangladeshi economies are reacting to inflation and the economic pressures caused by two major wars that have jolted energy markets.

Bangladesh is expected to have a GDP of $506.4bn in 2026, compared with India’s $4.15 trillion. But its lead in GDP per capita reverses when adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. On this measure, India is projected to have a GDP per capita at $12,998, compared with Bangladesh’s $10,884.

PPP is an economic metric that represents what money can actually buy in different countries after adjusting for the cost of living. The figures mean that Indians have a higher buying capacity than Bangladeshis.

The IMF projected India’s average consumer-price inflation at 5 percent, compared with 8.7 percent in Bangladesh, pointing to greater cost-of-living pressures in Dhaka.

India is relatively wealthier than Bangladesh and is home to a big industrial base, including its significant technology sector.

India’s economy is expected to grow by 7 percent in 2026, nearly twice Bangladesh’s 3.6 percent rate.

For context, the average per capita GDP in developing economies is about $7,746 – and the global average is about $15,889 – against Bangladesh’s $2,886 and India’s $2,749.

Where are India’s and Bangladesh’s economies expected to go?

In the next year, the IMF report projected that Bangladesh’s per capita GDP would reach $3,219, still higher than India’s $3,036 – a difference, according to the estimates, that should continue marginally in 2028.

In 2029, based on current growth forecasts, India’s per capita GDP of $3,661 would top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the IMF.

Experts noted that Bangladesh is facing a weaker near-term growth outlook, even as its projected GDP per capita edges above India’s.

But GDP per capita alone does not paint a complete economic picture because it conceals inequalities in income and wealth distribution. The dollar-denominated figure also changes with the exchange rate, which means that a change in a currency’s value can alter the relative numbers without a change in economic output.

In brief, the growth in Bangladesh’s economy in the past two decades has focused on export-oriented manufacturing, particularly its ready-made garment industry, which has been a major source of export earnings and employment, in addition to remittances from Bangladeshis working abroad.

Meanwhile, India has a diversified economy, with services playing a major role alongside manufacturing and agriculture. Its domestic market, technology and business services, industrial base and consumer demand provide multiple sources of economic activity.

In both countries, however, economic growth over the past decade has been unequal with increasing concentration in wealthier households.

Is Bangladesh a South Asian success story?

To some extent, yes, analysts said while expressing caution about unequal growth.

Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian economist, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s economy has shown consistent economic growth of 6 percent per annum alongside a long-term decline in population growth.

The country has also seen its manufacturing contribution to gross value added shoot up from 16.6 percent in 2014 to 22 percent in 2025, Mehrotra said. On the other hand, World Bank data showed India’s manufacturing value added falling from 15.1 percent of GDP in 2014 to 13.5 percent in 2024.

“That’s a positive side of export-oriented manufacturing growth that Bangladesh is getting right,” he said.

However, the global energy shock from the United States-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, has jolted Bangladesh.

Bangladesh imports 95 percent of its oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and much of these imports comes from the Middle East.

The ready‑made garment industry, which accounts for more than 80 percent of Bangladesh’s export earnings, has also been hit as its shipment routes via the Red Sea and the Middle East have been disrupted.

articles.body:
Lunedì 26 ottobre il presidente di Federchimica Francesco Buzzella riunirà le imprese a Milano: dopo i messaggi di Meloni, Metsola, Urso e Pichetto Fratin, attesi il presidente di Confindustria Emanuele Orsini e il ministro Tajani

Agli industriali della chimica lunedì, all’assemblea annuale al The mall di Milano, non mancheranno certo i temi da discutere, tra costi dell’energia e del sistema Ets, burocrazia, perdita di capacità produttiva in Europa e sempre maggiore aggressività dei competitor cinesi. Un insieme di questioni che mettono a rischio non solo la presenza industriale in Italia e in Europa, ma anche il mantenimento dello stato sociale che le ha caratterizzate fin qui e che in larga parte si deve anche alla manifattura. E quando si parla di manifattura non si può non parlare di chimica, visto che il settore è presente nel 95% dei manufatti e, con 60 miliardi di euro di fatturato e oltre 117mila addetti altamente qualificati, è la quinta industria del Paese. In Europa, l’Italia è il terzo produttore.

Se guardiamo alla produzione, l’anno si chiuderà, a conferma delle previsioni dei mesi scorsi, con il segno negativo e bisognerà aspettare il 2027 per vedere un lieve segnale positivo. In questa fase di grandi trasformazioni, il presidente di Federchimica, Francesco Buzzella, riunirà gli industriali per ascoltarli e portare avanti le loro istanze, approfittando anche della presenza del Presidente di Confindustria Emanuele Orsini e del ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani. I temi ancora al centro del dibattito restano i costi dell’energia e sistemi come l’Ets, che anche dopo il via libera del Parlamento europeo a più quote gratuite continuano ad essere fortemente critici per la competitività dell’industria chimica. Tanto più che la concorrenza cinese è sempre più agguerrita.

Per inquadrare il settore nella sua dimensione nazionale, europea ed internazionale ad aprire i lavori dell’assemblea di Federchimica saranno i messaggi della Presidente del Consiglio dei ministri, Giorgia Meloni, e della Presidente del Parlamento europeo, Roberta Metsola. Dopo gli interventi del ministro Tajani e di Orsini, arriveranno anche i messaggi del ministro delle imprese e del made in Italy, Adolfo Urso e di quello dell’Ambiente, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin. La giornata sarà chiusa da una tavola rotonda intitolata “Industria, salute, energia: quale Europa?” alla quale parteciperanno Ilaria Capua, professor e senior fellow of global health alla Johns Hopkins University Sais Europe, Davide Tabarelli, presidente di Nomisma Energia e Giulio Terzi di Sant’Agata, presidente della Commissione politiche Ue del Senato.

articles.body:
Lettera di Efic al commissario al commercio. Le imprese europee chiedono tutela e supporto a un’industria che dà lavoro a oltre 1 milione di persone

Non è un fenomeno nuovo in Europa: oggi se ne parla di più e c’è una maggiore sensibilità sul tema, perché all’aumento di importazioni di mobili dalla Cina si è aggiunto anche un forte calo delle esportazioni, che nei primi sette mesi dell’anno sono diminuite, per l’Italia, del 17,7% rispetto a luglio 2025.

La concorrenza dei prodotti cinesi sul mercato Ue - agguerrita sui prezzi e spesso sleale - è iniziata tuttavia diversi anni fa e ha creato non poche difficoltà ai produttori europei, in particolare in Germania, Francia e anche in Polonia, dove la gran parte della produzione nazionale è posizionata sul segmento medio.

L’impatto sul made in Italy

L’Italia, finora, sembrava essere rimasta al riparo, grazie a un sistema produttivo specializzato soprattutto nel design e nell’alto di gamma. Finora, appunto. Perché i dati di FederlegnoArredo sulle importazioni di mobili dalla Cina nel primo semestre fanno suonare più di un campanello d’allarme. Apparentemente, infatti, il dato sembra innocuo: il nostro Paese ha infatti importato tra gennaio e giugno di quest’anno prodotti per un valore di 1,1 miliardi di euro, una quota bassa sul totale di importazioni Ue (15,4 miliardi) e soprattutto in calo dell’1% rispetto al primo semestre del 2025. «Ma dietro questo dato cumulato si nascondono picchi registrati nei mesi di aprile, giugno, luglio e agosto, con incrementi rispettivamente del 19,6%, del 9%, del 20% e del 42%», osserva Claudio Feltrin, presidente della federazione.

Non solo: nello stesso periodo sono aumentate le importazioni di prodotti della filiera legno-arredo da altri Paesi asiatici, in particolare dal Vietnam, che lasciano pensare a fenomeni di triangolazione, soprattutto per alcune categorie (come i pavimenti in legno) su cui è entrata in vigore lo scorso anno una misura antidumping verso la Cina. Un altro indizio è il forte aumento di importazioni della filiera (+62,4%) registrato dai Paesi Bassi, dove si trova lo strategico porto di Rotterdam.

L’aumento dei volumi in entrata

Ma soprattutto, Feltrin invita a guardare e interpretare i dati sulle quantità in entrata: tra gennaio e luglio 2026, a fronte di un calo del 2,5% nei valori, l’Italia ha infatti importato dal Paese asiatico il 9,4% in più dei volumi. Elemento che solleva un altro tema, altrettanto e forse più grave: «Siamo di fronte a una concorrenza sleale, che rischia di mettere in ginocchio le nostre aziende già gravate dall’aumento dei costi produttivi per il caro energia - dice Feltrin -. La nostra filiera è sotto attacco in tutta Europa, come già è accaduto per l’automotive: molte aziende cinesi commercializzano in Europa prodotti, anche di buona qualità, a prezzi bassissimi, impossibili da praticare se, alle spalle, non avessero un governo che copre le perdite».

articles.body:
Gli operai lasciano le postazioni occupate. Lavoratori e sindacati mantengono alta l’attenzione e la mobilitazione in attesa del prossimo incontro

Stop all’occupazione del forno a 60 metri di altezza e massima attenzione in attesa del prossimo incontro previsto per fine mese. Quando si capirà se gli interventi annunciati per “salvare” l’Eurallumina di Portovesme potranno concretizzarsi. Ossia, lo stanziamento da parte dello Stato delle risorse necessarie per mandare avanti la fabbrica (che con gli impianti spenti e in attesa del progetto di rilancio da 350 milioni di euro, oggi si occupa della bonifica della falda) e pagare stipendi e fornitori.

L’incontro al Mimit

È quanto emerso dall’incontro tecnico al Mimit, convocato per fare il punto sullo stato della vertenza e poi aggiornato a fine mese. «È stato annunciato da parte del Mef l’impegno formale con una erogazione di risorse che auspichiamo siano sino al 31 dicembre da parte dello Stato - dice Nino D’Orso della Cisl regionale -. Ora si dovrà quantificare il fabbisogno e poi capire quante risorse serviranno, con una particolare attenzione alla questione ambientale». Non solo: «Inoltre è stato anche annunciato l’interesse da parte di tre potenziali investitori internazionali per rilevare lo stabilimento. A questo punto è necessario capire cosa sarà confermato nel corso della prossima convocazione per il 29 o 30 ottobre».

Corsa contro il tempo

Una corsa contro il tempo, per evitare il rischio di insolvenza dell’azienda che, sotto il controllo della russa Rusal si occupava, sino alla fermata del marzo 2009 per via degli alti costi energetici, della trasformazione della bauxite in allumina, costituendo il primo anello della filiera dell’alluminio. Da allora una serie di progetti per il rilancio, manifestazioni per sbloccare procedure ferme o al rilento.

L’esposizione dell’azienda

Da qualche tempo, però, l’azienda deve fare i conti con il congelamento delle risorse finanziarie disposto dall’autorità competente nell’ambito delle sanzioni alla Russia. Da un anno la Rusal ha smesso di versare gli oltre 2 milioni di euro al mese per tenere in piedi lo stabilimento sardo. «Tutte le risorse necessarie per garantire continuità e che dovrebbe erogare lo Stato, per tenere in piedi la fabbrica non sono arrivate - è la denuncia dei sindacati -. In questo contesto è naturalmente cresciuto il debito tanto che l’azienda è ora a rischio insolvenza».

Un’emergenza che ha spinto i lavoratori a occupare il forno di calcinazione a 60 metri di altezza alla vigilia dell’’incontro tecnico al Mimit.
